---
title: "Data-generating processes"
---

Suppose annotators judge the acceptability of a sentence on a four category scale. We observe the category, but the category alone does not say how sentence acceptability, response noise, and the scale boundaries combined to produce it. Writing code before answering that question can hide incompatible assumptions inside one function call.

A [**data-generating process**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-workflow.html) is an ordered account of the random choices and deterministic mappings that could produce an observation. The threshold account below gives a latent-variable representation of the [cumulative logit model](../regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd) introduced earlier. It is written before the joint distribution so that every later probability term has a stated role in the annotation process.

## State one step at a time

For a first model of the ordered judgment, consider the following process.

1. Each sentence $i$ has an unobserved acceptability value $\theta_i$.
2. A trial response $Z_{ij}$ varies around that value.
3. Fixed ordered thresholds map $Z_{ij}$ to the recorded category $Y_{ij}$.

This process intentionally omits stable annotator differences. Its purpose is to expose the item and observation rule before a later page extends the account.

To retain the earlier cumulative-logit response model, let trial variation follow a standard logistic distribution:

$$
Z_{ij}=\theta_i+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\varepsilon_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Logistic}(0,1).
$$

For four response categories, let $c_1<c_2<c_3$ be the thresholds. The recorded response is

$$
Y_{ij}=k
\quad\text{when}\quad
c_{k-1}<Z_{ij}\leq c_k,
$$

where $c_0=-\infty$ and $c_4=\infty$. The dependence sequence is

$$
\theta_i
\longrightarrow
Z_{ij}
\longrightarrow
Y_{ij}.
$$

The arrows describe an order of generation, not a chronology in the annotator's mind. They state which values are needed to generate each later value.

## Work through one response

Suppose one sentence has $\theta_i=.8$, and one trial receives noise $\varepsilon_{ij}=-.2$. Its latent response is

$$
Z_{ij}=.8-.2=.6.
$$

Let the thresholds be $c_1=-1$, $c_2=0$, and $c_3=1$. Since

$$
0<.6\leq1,
$$

the recorded category is $Y_{ij}=3$. The model interprets category 3 as the result of a latent response falling between the second and third thresholds. It does not interpret the numeral 3 as a direct measurement of $\theta_i$.

Different noise draws can yield different categories for the same sentence. If $\varepsilon_{ij}=.5$, then $Z_{ij}=1.3$ and the response becomes category 4. Trial variation is thus part of the measurement account rather than evidence that the sentence changed between presentations.

## Implement the generation in base R

```{r}
generate_ordered_response <- function(theta, noise, thresholds) {
  latent_response <- theta + noise
  response <- findInterval(latent_response, thresholds) + 1L

  data.frame(
    theta = theta,
    noise = noise,
    latent_response = latent_response,
    response = response
  )
}

generate_ordered_response(
  theta = 0.8,
  noise = -0.2,
  thresholds = c(-1, 0, 1)
)
```

The function accepts the random draw `noise` rather than generating it internally. This makes the hand calculation visible. A simulator would draw many noise values and then apply the same deterministic threshold mapping.

## A data-generating process makes commitments

The process says that noise enters before thresholding and that every response uses the same thresholds. If annotators differ in their scale use, common thresholds may fail. If a response is bounded and has meaningful endpoints, a latent ordered category process may not match the instrument. These are empirical and measurement commitments, not implementation details.

The process also brackets a question. It does not yet represent stable annotator tendencies. This omission is acceptable only because it is explicit and temporary. A later extension adds an annotator component after the joint distribution for the simpler process is clear.

## Account for every recorded variable

Every recorded variable should either appear in the data-generating process or be declared outside its scope. If confidence is recorded but omitted, the analysis should say that it does not model confidence. If a follow up question appears only after an affirmative gate, the display rule belongs in the process.

Conversely, every latent quantity needs a role. Adding an unobserved variable can make a model flexible while leaving its scale or meaning unidentified. A verbal label does not identify a latent variable.

## Every variable needs a role in the model

Every recorded or latent quantity must have a defined role in the generative process. An observed confidence score is omitted when the model silently ignores it while claiming to represent the complete instrument. A latent state is unidentified when it affects no observation or when several latent states make identical predictions.

The repair is a design decision. Give the variable a role in the data-generating process, narrow the model's claim so the variable is explicitly omitted, or remove an unnecessary latent quantity. Writing the process before code exposes the choice.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the generative order"}
1. Which value is generated directly from $\theta_i$ in the worked process?
2. Why can two responses to the same sentence differ under the model?
3. What model commitment is made by using one threshold vector for every response?
4. What happens when an observed variable has no defined role in the generative process?
:::

## Summing up

A data-generating process orders the random choices and mappings that connect a linguistic quantity to a recorded annotation. The order exposes assumptions before they are compressed into software. The next page translates each step into a factor in [one joint distribution](writing-a-joint-model.qmd).
